power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Aggression in the genus Pan (including bonobos and chimpanzees) remains a central puzzle in primatology and anthropology.

Traditionally framed as a dichotomy between "peaceful bonobos" and "violent chimpanzees," recent findings challenge this view by documenting coalitionary aggression, maternal cannibalism, and lethal intergroup encounters in bonobos, alongside evidence that captive chimpanzees and bonobos exhibit comparable aggression levels.
These observations highlight the importance of ecological context, demographic composition, and behavioral plasticity in shaping aggression.
We propose that species identity is a weaker predictor of aggression in Pan than socioecological, demographic, social, and neuroendocrine context.
While captivity offers methodological control, it also introduces confounds such as reduced group size, absence of fission-fusion dynamics, and enforced proximity.
Conversely, wild studies reveal the ecological pressures, territorial defense, resource distribution, and interspecies competition that drive variation in aggression.

Future research must integrate captive and free-ranging data through hybrid protocols, quantify ecological and demographic drivers, and explore neuroendocrine mechanisms underlying sex-specific aggression.

An integrative review on Pan aggression will refine our understanding of adaptive strategies, illuminate the evolutionary roots of human social conflict, and advance comparative models of primate behavior.

Aggression is a behavioral trait present across all phyla in the animal kingdom, from nonhuman animals to humans. Georgiev et al. (2013) proposed that aggression can be understood as an adaptive cost-benefit strategy in which the expression of aggression depends on the balance between its fitness benefits, such as access to resources, mates, territory, and social status, and its associated costs, including injury, energetic expenditure, stress, and damage to social relationships.

text.text: This framework predicts that variation in aggression among species reflects differences in ecological and social conditions rather than fixed behavioral predispositions.

Investigating aggression in non-human primates (NHPs) provides a crucial comparative framework for understanding the evolution of human aggressive behavior, particularly with regard to our closest phylogenetic relatives.

According to Holekamp & Strauss (2016) "aggression" is defined as "harmful, potentially harmful, or threatening behavior that is directed towards conspecifics, and tends to increase the distance between an attacker and its opponent".

text.text: For detailed definitions and classifications of the various aggression types included in the Pan ethogram, we direct readers to Nishida et al. (1999); Stevens et al. (2023).

text.text: Bonobos (Pan paniscus) and chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) live in multi-male/multi-female social systems characterized by male philopatry, which implies female dispersal in groups with fission-fusion dynamics.
They are our closest living relatives, sharing a common ancestor with humans and exhibiting approximately 97-98% genetic similarity, as well as notable physiological parallels (Prüfer et al., 2012).
text.formatted: They are our closest living relatives, sharing a common ancestor with humans and exhibiting approximately 97-98% genetic similarity, as well as notable physiological parallels <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Prüfer et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Although they have both similar social systems, the divergence remains significant.

Bonobos are expected to align more closely with the "empathizing" trajectory, displaying higher levels of cooperation and affiliation, while chimpanzees would align more with the "systemising" trajectory, showing -among othershigher levels of aggression and competitive behavior (MacLean, 2016).
text.formatted: Bonobos are expected to align more closely with the "empathizing" trajectory, displaying higher levels of cooperation and affiliation, while chimpanzees would align more with the "systemising" trajectory, showing -among othershigher levels of aggression and competitive behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(MacLean, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: By acting as a natural ecological barrier separating the two species of the genus Pan, the Congo River has facilitated substantial divergence in their morphological and cognitive characteristics, as well as in their social organization.

According to the self-domestication hypothesis (Hare et al., 2012), bonobos have retained a suite of neotenic (juvenile) traits, including morphological characteristics, lower testosterone levels, reduced aggression, and higher levels of social play compared to chimpanzees-even in adulthood.
text.formatted: According to the self-domestication hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hare et al., 2012)</ref>, bonobos have retained a suite of neotenic (juvenile) traits, including morphological characteristics, lower testosterone levels, reduced aggression, and higher levels of social play compared to chimpanzees-even in adulthood.

text.text: In addition, the authors argued that this behavior may be explained by the fact that the distribution range of bonobos (a species endemic to Democratic Republic of the Congo, DRC) does not overlap with that of any other great ape, because of the Congo River, thereby reducing interspecies competition.
In contrast, chimpanzees inhabit the equatorial belt of Africa north of the Congo River, ranging across habitats from dense equatorial rainforests to seasonal savannas.
This natural environmental barrier may have shaped the aggressive traits displayed by chimpanzees relative to gorillas, with whom they share the same distribution range.

Interspecific encounters can escalate to lethal attacks, as reported by Southern et al. (2021) in Loango National Park, Gabon, where a coalition of adult male chimpanzees killed a juvenile gorilla during a territorial patrol.

text.text: Comparative studies of wild populations have demonstrated that male chimpanzees exhibit higher rates of aggression, more frequent coalitionary behavior, and stronger affiliative bonds with other males than bonobos, suggesting important species differences in the social functions of aggression and cooperation (Surbeck et al., 2017).

text.text: The present review seeks to move beyond the traditional dichotomy of "peaceful bonobos"
versus "violent chimpanzees" by situating aggression within an integrative evolutionary framework.
Specifically, we ask whether aggression in Pan reflects adaptive strategies shaped by ecological constraints, reproductive pressures, social organization, and neuroendocrine mechanisms (Box 1).

We hypothesize that interspecific differences in aggression between bonobos and chimpanzees are primarily explained by ecological, demographic, social, and neuroendocrine factors interacting with environmental context rather than by fixed behavioral predispositions.

Understanding how NHPs negotiate dynamic socio-ecological contexts by weighing biological costs and advantages is crucial to comprehending the multifaceted nature of aggression and social behavior in the genus Pan (Garcia et al., 2021).

text.text: Primates manage resource competition, reproductive constraints, and social disputes by using flexible cognitive processes, such as value-based decision-making and long-term planning, rather than strict behavioral reflexes (Garcia et al., 2021).

text.text: According to this evolutionary framework, offensive aggression functions as a specialized biobehavioral system that has been molded by natural selection to react directly to territorial, resource, and status challenges.

Aggression is increasingly recognized as a multidimensional phenomenon shaped by interactions among developmental, physiological, social, and evolutionary processes.
Rather than reflecting a single behavioral trait, aggressive behavior emerges through the interaction of endocrine mechanisms, social experience, dominance relationships, and ecological pressures.

text.text: In both daily foraging situations and macro-level population dynamics, ecological constraints -primarily the spatial distribution, seasonality, and patchiness of food resources-act as a main evolutionary catalyst shaping aggressive behaviors in the genus Pan.
At the local scale, the reliability of resources directly influences social unity and intra-group competitive dynamics.

While the ubiquitous availability of protein-rich Terrestrial Herbaceous Vegetation (THV) in bonobo habitats buffers against foraging stress and promotes long-term female gregariousness and coalitions by attending mixed-sex parties without incurring large costs from contest and scramble competition, while chimpanzees' dependence on seasonal variation in food availability leads to more flexible fission-fusion social systems have been primary topics in socio-ecological comparisons to address the differences in genus Pan (Furuichi, 2009).

text.text: These ecological factors regulate the cost-benefit trade-offs of intergroup violence and establish home-range carrying capacity at the landscape scale.
Chimpanzees use numerical asymmetries during border patrols to aggressively extend territorial boundaries when resource scarcity imposes energetic costs.

text.text: Evidence from bonobos suggests that the function of aggression may differ substantially from that observed in chimpanzees.

At LuiKotale, Hohmann et al. (2019) found that although male bonobos occasionally directed intense aggression toward immature individuals, the behavior did not conform to predictions of the adaptive infanticide hypothesis.

text.text: Aggression was directed primarily toward older, weaned immatures rather than dependent infants, males did not preferentially target unrelated offspring, and no lethal outcomes were observed.

These findings indicate that male aggression in bonobos may serve functions other than infanticide, including the regulation of dominance relationships, dispersal processes, or competition for future resources.

Yet paternal infanticide has not been documented. Walker et al. (2021) described in the Kasekela group at Gombe an attempted case in which an adult male, identified as the father, joined his mother, who initiated the attack on the infant of another adult female.

By contrast, male infanticide in mammalian societies is well documented, whereas cases committed by females remain very rare among group-living primates.

text.text: They found no correlation between food scarcity and the occurrence of infanticide, and attackers were not in energetically costly reproductive states.
However, infanticide was significantly more likely when the female-to-male ratio was higher.
Moreover, females were more prone to attack mothers with whom they experienced greater competition, as indicated by core area overlap.
Females occupying higher dominance ranks are more likely to prevail over lower-ranking females when initiating aggression.
In female-dominated societies such as that of bonobos, male-male aggression does not appear to function to prevent other males from associating with females, given the absence of sexual coercion.

A similar pattern is observed in other female-dominated mammals in which females are as aggressive as, or more aggressive than, males, such as spotted hyena, Crocuta crocuta (Curren et al., 2015). Furuichi (2011) proposed that the relatively peaceful nature of bonobo society is largely rooted in female social strategies.

text.text: Female bonobos maintain strong affiliative bonds, form coalitions, exert influence over group movements, and provide support to their adult sons, while prolonged pseudo-estrus reduces male reproductive competition and sexual coercion.

Together, these interacting mechanisms enhance female social influence, promote group cohesion, and contribute to the higher levels of tolerance typically observed in bonobos compared with chimpanzees.
In bonobos, females form powerful coalitions among non-relatives to subordinate males and gain priority of access to resources.

Evidence from LuiKotale indicates that maternal support plays a central role in male bonobo social dynamics: mothers frequently associate with their adult sons, provide agonistic support during conflicts with other males, and enhance the mating success of low-and mid-ranking sons (Surbeck et al., 2011), suggesting that dominance trajectories and reproductive opportunities are shaped not only by male competitive ability but also by female social leverage and maternal support.

text.text: Although chimpanzees and bonobos share fission-fusion dynamics and male philopatry, divergent social structures and physiological traits shape their respective capacities for peaceful coexistence.

As Clay et al. (2016) highlight, bonobo society is catalyzed by prolonged female sexual swellings and concealed ovulation, which foster female-female aggregation, secure feeding priority, and reduce inter-male competition.

text.text: Furthermore, while both species engage in conflict resolution strategies like reconciliation and consolation, bonobos uniquely integrate high levels of socio-sexual behavior as a mechanism for social tension regulation.
In contrast, social mechanisms in chimpanzees are structured around male-male cooperation and intense competition.

Comparative evidence from wild populations indicates that male chimpanzees engage more frequently in male-male coalitions and devote a greater proportion of their affiliative interactions to other males through grooming and post-conflict reconciliation, whereas bonobo males form substantially fewer coalitions with one another (Surbeck et al., 2017).

text.text: Consequently, male-male aggression in chimpanzees is driven primarily by territorial defense and reproductive strategies, including the use of sexual coercion against females.

Female immigration in this species is a high-risk process in which young females face marked hostility from resident females competing for territory and resources (Walker et al., 2021), whereas native males exhibit reproductive tolerance.

text.text: New immigrants receive significantly more aggression from other immigrants than do established immigrants, though new and established immigrants are treated equally by adult natal males.

These contrasting patterns highlight how divergent social strategies-female-centered affiliation and appeasement in bonobos versus male-driven alliances and resource competition in chimpanzees-shape interspecific variation in social cohesion and conflict.
Oxytocin (OT) is a neuropeptide hormone involved in a range of functions of sociality in animal systems, especially in affiliative behaviors, such as dyadic relationship qualities.
In this section, we will discuss the way OT modulates empathy and consolation.

text.text: Current evidence suggests that OT modulates empathy by enhancing sensitivity to socially relevant cues and increasing emotional attunement to others.
This is reflected in reduced self-interest, greater prosocial engagement, and enhanced emotional empathy.

Importantly, these effects are highly context-dependent and are shaped by both individual characteristics (e.g., sex, personality, anxiety, and developmental history) and environmental conditions, particularly social and emotional contexts (reviewed in Yao & Kendrick, 2025).

The steroid hormone testosterone (T) is well established as a key modulator of aggressive behavior, as demonstrated by extensive empirical research, in non-human animals while in humans that link is more controversial (e.g., Book et al., 2001; reviewed in Geniole et al., 2020).

text.text: However, the behavioral effects of T are not uniform across species. Lynn (2008) argued that many vertebrates exhibit behavioral insensitivity to T, indicating that circulating hormone concentrations alone do not reliably predict aggression or other social behaviors.

text.text: Instead, species-specific ecological pressures, life-history strategies, and variation in receptor sensitivity may modulate how T influences behavior.
This perspective suggests that differences between bonobos and chimpanzees may arise not only from variation in hormone levels, but also from differences in physiological responsiveness to androgens.
Recent evidence further suggests that the relationship between T and aggression is considerably more complex than traditionally assumed.
In a large meta-analysis, Geniole et al. (2020) found that baseline T and T reactivity were positively associated with aggression in men, but the observed effects were relatively weak.
Moreover, experimental administration of T did not consistently increase aggressive behavior.

The authors concluded that T-related effects on aggression are strongly influenced by social context, individual characteristics, and situational factors, highlighting that T should be viewed as a context-dependent modulator rather than a direct biological determinant of aggression.

Evidence from wild chimpanzees further supports a neuroendocrine basis for aggression in reproductive contexts. Muller & Wrangham (2004) found that male chimpanzees exhibited elevated T levels during periods when sexually receptive parous females were present, coinciding with increased rates of male-male aggression.

These findings suggest that T is more closely associated with competitive aggression related to reproductive opportunities than with sexual behavior itself, supporting the view that neuroendocrine mechanisms play a central role in mediating context-dependent aggression in Pan.
On the other hand, neither in captivity nor in the wild, T levels in bonobos suggest an association with only a limited subset of aggressive behaviors.

Most forms of aggression appear to be more strongly influenced by social factors than by endocrine status, although elevated T is linked to increased responsiveness to provocation and certain display behaviors.

Overall, T appears to exert contrasting social effects across Pan species, amplifying coalitionary aggression and reproductive competition in chimpanzees, while in bonobos its effects are moderated by strong affiliative bonds and mitigates reproductive coercion.
Recent evidence from humans indicates that T and OT interact rather than acting independently in the regulation of competitive and aggression-related behaviors.
In an experimental model of intergroup conflict, increases in T reactivity predicted costly competitive behavior toward outgroups in males, whereas OT administration attenuated this relationship.
Notably, these effects were sex-specific, with no comparable T-dependent pattern observed in females (Cherki et al., 2024).

text.text: Although similar mechanisms remain largely unexplored in bonobos and chimpanzees, these findings provide a valuable theoretical framework for understanding how interacting neuroendocrine pathways may contribute to context-dependent variation in aggression across Pan species.

text.text: Importantly, skepticism regarding the traditional bonobo-chimpanzee dichotomy is not new.

More than two decades ago, Stanford (1998) argued that the behavioral differences between the two Pan species had often been overstated and that many apparent contrasts reflected differences in research intensity, sampling history, and ecological context rather than fundamentally distinct behavioral syndromes.

text.text: He suggested that bonobos and chimpanzees share a broader repertoire of social and aggressive behaviors than commonly assumed, a view that anticipated recent findings emphasizing behavioral plasticity and substantial withinspecies variation.

Comparative analyses across the Pan lineage further suggest that behavioral variation cannot be adequately explained by species membership alone. Kovalaskas et al. (2021) argued that ecological conditions, social environments, and population-specific factors generate substantial behavioral diversity within both bonobos and chimpanzees, limiting the explanatory power of simple species-level contrasts.

text.text: Their findings support the view that aggression and social behavior in Pan are best interpreted along a continuum of behavioral plasticity rather than as fixed species-specific syndromes.
This perspective is supported by recent empirical evidence challenging species-wide generalizations.

Using standardized focal-follow data collected from wild populations, Mouginot et al. (2024) found that male bonobos at Kokolopori exhibited higher rates of male-male aggression than male chimpanzees at Gombe, even when analyses were restricted to contact aggression.

text.text: However, male chimpanzees engaged in coalitionary aggression far more frequently than bonobos.
Moreover, in both species, more aggressive males achieved greater mating success.

These findings suggest that the frequency, intensity, and social consequences of aggression do not necessarily co-vary and should be interpreted within the broader context of reproductive competition and coalitionary behavior.
These contrasting findings suggest that variation among populations may rival or even exceed average differences between species.
Ecological conditions, demographic composition, social relationships, and local selective pressures likely shape the expression of aggression in both bonobos and chimpanzees.
Consequently, aggression in Pan may be better understood as a context-dependent and plastic behavioral strategy rather than as a fixed species-specific trait.

These observations suggest that coalitionary aggression can emerge from shifts in social relationships and group structure, supporting the view that aggression in Pan is a flexible and context-dependent behavioral strategy rather than a fixed species-specific predisposition.
Moving from active aggressive displays to feeding contexts, recent evidence indicates that behavioral differences between bonobos and chimpanzees may be less pronounced than traditionally assumed.

These results challenge species-level generalizations and emphasize the importance of local social dynamics in shaping behavioral expression in Pan.
This pattern of overlapping behavior extends beyond social tolerance and co-feeding.
Recent evidence suggests that the limitations of species-level dichotomies extend beyond aggression and social tolerance.

The authors concluded that behavioral variation within species may exceed differences between species, reinforcing the view that socio-emotional traits in Pan are highly flexible and context dependent.
Collectively, these findings indicate that behavioral variation within bonobos and chimpanzees may, in some cases, exceed differences between species.

Across aggression, social tolerance, and empathy-related behaviors, species membership appears to be a weaker predictor of behavioral expression than the interacting effects of socioecological, demographic, social, and neuroendocrine factors.

This review is consistent with the review of Gruber & Clay (2016), who argued that comparisons between bonobos and chimpanzees have historically overstated species differences while underestimating substantial variation within species.

text.text: The authors emphasized that behavioral diversity across Pan populations reflects a continuum shaped by ecological and social factors rather than a simple opposition between two fixed behavioral syndromes.
Consequently, understanding aggression in Pan requires consideration of both interspecific and intrapopulation variation, as well as the ecological conditions under which behavior is expressed.
As emphasized by Pusey (2022), the contrast between "warlike" chimpanzees and "peacemaking" bonobos should not be interpreted as a simple species-level dichotomy.

text.text: While chimpanzees typically exhibit territorial behavior and hostile intergroup interactions, bonobos may engage in prolonged and tolerant encounters with neighbouring groups.
Importantly, evidence suggests that these interacting bonobo groups remain socially distinct, indicating that intergroup tolerance is genuine rather than an artefact of group subdivision.

The ecological and demographic factors underlying these differences remain debated, but variation in resource distribution, population density, home-range overlap, and territorial defendability have been proposed as key drivers.
Together, these observations support the view that aggression and tolerance in Pan are flexible socioecological strategies rather than fixed species-specific traits.

This review further supports the need to interpret aggression within a broader socioecological framework and highlights the importance of considering environmental context when comparing captive and wild populations.

text.text: In other words, the captive environment itself may constitute a factor underlying the behavioral differences observed between species, when contrasted with those expressed under natural conditions.

It remains challenging to compare data from captive environments with those from wild populations due to the absence of hybrid protocols, which can lead to underscore aggression in Pan reduced to a simple dichotomy of 'peaceful bonobos' versus 'violent chimpanzees'.
For future directions, the research should quantify ecological drivers such as resource distribution and prey availability, and examine the neuroendocrine bases of sex-specific aggression.

Such an integrative approach will clarify whether aggression in Pan reflects adaptive strategies, ecological constraints, or evolutionary plasticity, and in turn, illuminate the roots of human social conflict.
Captivity may alter the socioecological conditions that regulate aggression and therefore complicate direct comparisons with wild populations.
It is noteworthy that there is still an imbalance in the sampling effort of current comparisons between chimpanzees and bonobos.

While data on chimpanzees come from over twenty longterm locations throughout Africa, long-term behavioral data on bonobos come from just three to four continually investigated sites (e.g., Wamba, Lomako, LuiKotale, and Kokolopori).
Our comprehension of the entire range of male-male violence in Pan may be skewed by this imbalance, especially when it comes to uncommon behaviors like deadly coalitionary aggression.
To test the context-dependent model presented here, other bonobo populations and standardized behavioral protocols must be included in future research.

We propose a series of additional testable predictions that may further inform ongoing debates in primatology and anthropology regarding the extent to which bonobos and chimpanzees differ in their propensity for aggressive behavior.
Prediction 1.
Socioecological context will explain more variation in aggression than species identity.
Prediction 2.
Bonobos and chimpanzees exposed to similar ecological conditions will exhibit more similar aggression profiles than predicted by the traditional aggression dichotomy.
Prediction 3.
Coalition structure and maternal support will predict dominance outcomes and aggressive behavior.
Prediction 4.
Variation in oxytocin and testosterone pathways will be associated with context-dependent variation in aggression.
Prediction 5.
Infanticide, cannibalism, and intergroup violence will be better predicted by ecological and demographic variables than by species membership.
Early studies contributed to the widespread portrayal of bonobos as peaceful and chimpanzees as inherently aggressive.
However, accumulating evidence from both captive and wild populations suggests that aggression in Pan is best understood as a flexible and context-dependent behavioral strategy.

The marked variation in lethal aggression observed among chimpanzee groups, together with recent findings from bonobos, indicates that differences among populations may equal or even exceed average species differences.

Therefore, the traditional bonobo-chimpanzee aggression dichotomy may partly reflect observer bias generated by uneven field effort and sampling intensity, rather than a fixed species-level difference.

Rather than representing opposite ends of a behavioral continuum, bonobos and chimpanzees appear to share a common behavioral repertoire whose expression is shaped by interacting ecological, demographic, social, and neuroendocrine factors.

These observations highlight the major role of local socioecological conditions in shaping aggressive behavior and support the view that aggression in Pan is better explained by behavioral plasticity than by fixed species-specific predispositions.
Understanding this variation will improve comparative models of primate social evolution and provide new insights into the evolutionary roots of human conflict.
